summary: Defines an architecture for providing scalable service differentiation in the Internet. It describes how traffic is classified and marked at the edges and given different treatment in the middle of the network. It is informational and updated by RFC 3260.

plainLanguage.summary: Differentiated Services lets a network treat some packets better than others without checking every flow at every router. At the edge, each packet is marked with a class, and inside the network each class gets the same forwarding treatment. This keeps the busy core simple and still lets providers sell different levels of service.

questions: what is the differentiated services architecture
how does diffserv provide quality of service
subtitle: How to give some packets better treatment than others by marking them at the edge and forwarding each class the same way inside the network.

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a way to offer different levels of service to different traffic without keeping per-flow state in the core routers, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: Traffic is classified, marked and conditioned at the edges of a domain, and core routers apply one of a small set of per-hop behaviors to each marked traffic aggregate.
tldr.outcome: The architecture became the basis of DiffServ, separating the service from the forwarding behavior and allowing many services to be built on a few building blocks; RFC 2475 is Informational and updated by RFC 3260.

sections.title: Purpose and Design Goals
sections.content:
This memo defines an architecture for scalable service differentiation in the Internet. A service describes significant characteristics of packet transmission in one direction across paths, in quantitative or statistical terms such as throughput, delay, jitter and loss, or as a relative priority for access to resources. Differentiation exists to accommodate different application needs and user expectations, and to permit differentiated pricing.

The architecture works by shifting complex work to the edges. Classification and conditioning run only at network boundary nodes, while per-hop behaviors apply to aggregates of traffic that have been marked using the DS field in the IPv4 or IPv6 header. No per-application flow or per-customer state is kept in the core. The RFC keeps a clear distinction between the service given to a traffic aggregate, the conditioning and per-hop behaviors that realize it, the DS field value used to select a per-hop behavior, and the node mechanisms that implement it.

The requirements section adds that the design should work with existing applications without changing host software or APIs, avoid hop-by-hop signaling, keep only a small set of forwarding behaviors, use aggregated classification state in the core, interoperate reasonably with nodes that do not implement differentiated services, and allow incremental deployment. A comparison with other approaches shows this architecture as a refinement of relative priority marking, and different from service marking, label switching, and Integrated Services with RSVP. The architecture provides differentiation in one direction of flow and is asymmetric; a symmetric architecture was a topic of research outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can promise different quality to different customers, but only if the routers in the middle stay simple. This design moves the hard work to the edges and gives the core a few easy jobs, so it keeps working as the network grows.

sections.title: Domains, Regions and Nodes
sections.content:
A DS domain is a contiguous set of nodes that run a common service provisioning policy and a common set of per-hop behavior groups. It normally belongs to one administration, such as an organization's intranet or an ISP, and has a well-defined boundary of DS boundary nodes that classify and possibly condition traffic entering the domain. Nodes inside the domain choose the forwarding behavior for a packet from its DS codepoint, using either the recommended codepoint-to-PHB mapping or a locally customized one. A DS domain may contain non-DS-compliant nodes, but that can give unpredictable performance and make service level agreements hard to meet.

Nodes are named by their role. DS boundary nodes connect the domain to other DS or non-DS-capable domains; DS interior nodes connect only to nodes in the same domain. A boundary node acts as the DS ingress node for traffic entering the domain and as the DS egress node for traffic leaving it; its ingress responsibility is to make entering traffic conform to the traffic conditioning agreement with the other domain. A host may act as its own boundary node; if it does not, the closest DS node does.

A DS region is a set of contiguous DS domains that can carry differentiated services over paths spanning them. The domains in a region may support different PHB groups and mappings, so peering domains establish a peering SLA that defines how transit traffic is conditioned at the boundary. Several domains may adopt the same policy and mappings, which removes the need for conditioning between them.
sections.plainLanguage: A DS domain is one operator's set of routers that share the same rules. Edge nodes decide how each entering packet is marked, and inner nodes simply look at that mark to choose how to forward it.

sections.title: Classification and Traffic Conditioning
sections.content:
Differentiated services cross a domain boundary through a service level agreement (SLA) between an upstream network and a downstream DS domain. The traffic conditioning agreement (TCA) derived from that SLA says how traffic is classified, marked and conditioned. Two kinds of classifier select packets: the BA (behavior aggregate) classifier looks only at the DS codepoint, while the MF (multi-field) classifier looks at a combination of header fields such as source and destination addresses, the DS field, protocol ID, source and destination ports, and the incoming interface. Classification rules should authenticate the information they use.

A traffic profile describes the temporal properties of a stream, such as rate and burst size, and decides whether a packet is in-profile or out-of-profile. An example in the RFC is a token bucket profile, written as codepoint equals X with bucket rate r and burst size b; packets that arrive when too few tokens remain are out-of-profile. In-profile packets may pass unchanged or be re-marked; out-of-profile packets may be shaped (delayed until they fit), policed (dropped), re-marked, or forwarded while triggering accounting, and may be mapped to an inferior behavior aggregate.

A traffic conditioner contains up to four elements. A meter measures the stream against the profile and passes its state to the other elements. A marker sets the DS codepoint, adding the packet to a behavior aggregate. A shaper delays packets to bring the stream into profile, and a dropper discards packets to do the same, which is called policing. When packets leave a boundary node's conditioner, their DS codepoint must be set appropriately. Conditioning is usually placed at ingress and egress boundary nodes, though it can also appear at traffic sources, in interior nodes, or in non-DS-capable domains for pre-marking.
sections.plainLanguage: At the edge, the network decides which class each packet belongs to, measures how much traffic each class is sending, and marks, delays or drops packets so the traffic fits what the customer paid for.

sections.title: Per-Hop Behaviors
sections.content:
A per-hop behavior (PHB) is the externally observable forwarding behavior a DS node applies to a behavior aggregate. It is the means by which a node allocates buffer and bandwidth among competing aggregates. Useful distinctions appear mainly when several aggregates compete for those resources. A simple example is a PHB that guarantees a minimal bandwidth allocation of X percent of a link over a reasonable time interval; a more complex one adds proportional fair sharing of any excess capacity. Behavior may also depend on constraints on the traffic characteristics of the aggregate.

PHBs are described in terms of observable behavior, not implementation. They are usually specified as a PHB group, a set that must be specified and implemented together because of a shared constraint such as a queue scheduling or buffer management policy; a single PHB is the special case of a group with one member. The same node may implement several PHB groups at once, and a group definition should say how it coexist with others.

The RFC also lists guidelines for specifying new PHB groups. A group must name a recommended DS codepoint from the space reserved for standard mappings, assigned by the IANA; deciding a packet's PHB must not require looking beyond the DS field. A specification should include an overview and problem statement, the number of PHBs and their interactions, behavior when constraints are violated, whether it is for general or local use, circumstances for re-marking within the group, tunneling implications, conformance requirements, security implications, and management considerations, with appendices recommended for services, link-layer mappings and higher-layer protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: A per-hop behavior is the promise a single router makes about how it forwards one class of marked packets, such as giving it at least a share of the link. Behaviors are described by what an observer can measure, not by how they are built.

sections.title: Legacy Nodes and Multicast
sections.content:
A non-DS-compliant node does not interpret the DS field as defined in the DS field specification or does not implement the standard PHBs. A legacy node is the special case that implements IPv4 Precedence as defined in the IPv4 specification and router requirements but is otherwise not DS-compliant. The IPv4 Precedence values are intentionally compatible with the Class Selector codepoints, so a legacy node can be an acceptable choice if the domain restricts itself to those codepoints, though the legacy node may or may not interpret the other TOS bits, which can make forwarding unpredictable.

Service quality can break down when traffic crosses a non-DS-compliant node or a non-DS-capable domain. On lightly loaded high-speed links the effect may be negligible, but a node without PHB forwarding can make low-delay, low-loss or provisioned-bandwidth services impossible across the paths that cross it. For a non-DS-capable domain, a DS domain may negotiate how its egress traffic is marked; a domain without knowledge of the downstream may re-mark codepoints to zero and rely on best-effort treatment. Traffic coming from a non-DS-capable domain is conditioned at the DS ingress node according to the appropriate SLA or policy.

Multicast raises two problems. Because packets can be replicated and take several paths, and group membership can be dynamic, it is hard to predict the resources multicast will consume, which makes quantitative guarantees to multicast senders difficult; codepoints and PHBs may need to be reserved for unicast. And a multicast packet may leave through several egress nodes peering with different downstream domains, so its codepoint must not request a service that violates a peering SLA. The RFC suggests a separate peering SLA for multicast or dedicated codepoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Older routers that only understand the older IPv4 priority bits can still work if the network restricts itself to compatible marks. Multicast is harder because packets are copied to many places, so their resource use is hard to predict.

sections.title: Theft, Denial of Service and Tunnels
sections.content:
The primary security concern is theft of service. Because service level is shown mainly by the DS field, an adversary can change a packet's DS codepoint or inject packets with high-priority codepoints to get better treatment. Pushed to its limit, this depletes resources for other traffic and becomes a denial-of-service attack. The defense is traffic conditioning at DS boundary nodes together with the security and integrity of the network infrastructure.

Ingress nodes are the main line of defense: they must condition all entering traffic so its codepoints conform to the applicable TCAs and the domain's provisioning policy, discarding or correcting unacceptable codepoints, for example resetting them to the Default PHB. Any traffic-originating node is an ingress node for its own traffic. Traffic authentication may be needed to validate the use of some codepoints, by technical means such as IPsec or non-technical ones such as knowing the inbound link has a single customer. Interior nodes may use the DS field without checking it, though they may make some checks; a link that cannot be secured against codepoint modification or injection should be treated as a boundary link. Auditable failures should be logged with the time, the source and destination addresses, and the offending codepoint.

On IPsec, the DS field is not included in IPsec's cryptographic calculations, so a network node changing it cannot break IPsec's integrity checks, but IPsec also gives no protection against such changes. In tunnel mode, intermediate nodes act on the outer header's DS field. A tunnel egress node is the DS ingress node for traffic leaving the tunnel unless a sufficiently strong integrity check lets it trust the inner header's DS field; a secure IPsec tunnel can therefore protect otherwise insecure internal links. The document makes no change to the IPsec rule that the inner header's DS field is not changed by decapsulation. Auditing is optional but, where implemented, an administrator must be able to enable or disable it.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could steal a better class of service by faking the mark on their packets, so edge routers check marks carefully. Encryption can protect the mark in transit, but it does not stop someone from changing the mark before or around the encrypted part.
